Inventory Turnover: Are You Moving Stock or Just Storing It?
Inventory is not just stock in a warehouse.
It is cash locked inside boxes.
One of the simplest ways to check whether inventory is healthy is through:
Inventory Turnover - This metric tells how many times a company sells and replaces its inventory during a period.
In simple words:  How fast is your inventory moving?
Main Formula:
Inventory Turnover = COGS / Average Inventory
Average Inventory = (Beginning Inventory + Ending Inventory) / 2
Example:
COGS = $1,000,000
Beginning Inventory = $200,000
Ending Inventory = $300,000
Average Inventory = $250,000
Inventory Turnover = 1,000,000 / 250,000 = 4 times
This means inventory was sold and replaced 4 times during the period.
Why It Matters?
Low inventory turnover may mean:
❌ Overstocking
❌ Slow-moving items
❌ Poor demand planning
❌ Cash tied up in stock
❌ Higher storage cost
Very high turnover may mean:
⚠️ Stockout risk
⚠️ Low safety stock
⚠️ Missed sales
⚠️ Replenishment pressure
So the goal is not always the highest turnover.
The goal is the right turnover.
Read It with Other KPIs
Inventory turnover should be compared with:
✅ Service level
✅ Stockout rate
✅ Gross margin
✅ Forecast accuracy
✅ Carrying cost
✅ Slow-moving inventory
Inventory turnover is not just a finance metric.
It is a supply chain health signal.
Inventory that moves too slowly hurts cash.
Inventory that moves too fast without control hurts service.
The real target is: Right stock. Right speed. Right service. Right margin.

🚢 How LPG Vessels Keep Global Energy Moving

Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) plays a crucial role in the global energy mix, providing a reliable source of fuel for households, industries, transportation, and petrochemical production.

Behind this global trade is a specialized fleet of LPG carriers designed to transport propane and butane safely and efficiently across international markets.

Key highlights of LPG shipping:

🔹 LPG is transported in liquid form under pressure or at low temperatures to maximize cargo capacity.
🔹 Specialized cargo tanks and containment systems ensure safe storage throughout the voyage.
🔹 Advanced loading, discharge, and vapor-handling systems maintain operational efficiency and cargo integrity.
🔹 Multiple safety layers, including gas detection, pressure relief systems, and double-hull designs, help protect both crew and environment.
🔹 LPG carriers connect major exporting nations in the Middle East and the United States with key importing markets across Asia and Europe.

As global demand for cleaner-burning fuels and petrochemical feedstocks continues to grow, LPG shipping remains an essential component of international energy trade and supply chain resilience.

🌍 From production terminals to end users, LPG vessels are a perfect example of how specialized maritime logistics enable global energy security.

There are countless articles about Lean.

How to implement Lean.
The biggest implementation mistakes.
The best Lean tools.
How to reduce waste.
How to increase productivity.

All of these topics matter.

But today, I’d like to share something different.

No process is ever perfect, and that’s exciting—not frustrating.

2️⃣ Small improvements create extraordinary results.

A 1% improvement repeated every day becomes a significant competitive advantage over time.

3️⃣ Lean gives everyone a voice.

The best ideas rarely come from the boardroom. They come from the people doing the work every day.

4️⃣ Problems become opportunities.

Instead of asking, “Who’s responsible?” Lean encourages us to ask, “What can we learn?”

5️⃣ Data replaces opinions.

Good decisions are based on facts, observation, and understanding—not assumptions.

6️⃣ Leadership means serving others.

The best Lean leaders remove obstacles, coach their teams, and help people succeed.

7️⃣ Improvement is never finished.

Reaching today’s target simply creates tomorrow’s opportunity.

8️⃣ Lean develops people, not just processes.

The greatest return on any improvement initiative is a team that has learned how to solve problems independently.

9️⃣ Simplicity wins.

The best solutions are often the simplest ones—clear standards, visual management, and disciplined daily habits.

🔟 Lean creates a culture, not just results.

Better quality, lower costs, and higher productivity are outcomes. The real achievement is building an environment where people continuously improve together.

🌱🪴🎯From Lean Practitioner to Lean Manager: What Skills Should Each Level Have?

In my previous article, I shared the different roles and responsibilities of a Lean Practitioner, Lean Specialist, Lean Expert, and Lean Manager.

A question followed naturally:
What are the minimum skills expected at each level?

While every organization has its own competency framework, I believe the progression should look something like this.

1️⃣Lean Practitioner – Learn and Apply

A Lean Practitioner doesn’t need to know every Lean tool. They need to understand why Lean exists and consistently apply its principles.

Minimum skills
• Understanding of Lean principles and the 8 wastes
• 5S, Visual Management and Standard Work
• Basic problem solving (PDCA, 5 Why)
• Ability to identify improvement opportunities
• Teamwork and willingness to learn
• Basic data collection and interpretation

At this level, curiosity and discipline are often more valuable than technical expertise.


2️⃣Lean Specialist – Coach and Facilitate

The Specialist’s role shifts from improving their own work to helping others improve.

Minimum skills
• Kaizen facilitation
• Value Stream Mapping
• Root Cause Analysis
• A3 thinking
• Training and coaching techniques
• Change management fundamentals
• Presentation and facilitation skills
• Basic project management

A great Specialist develops people, not just processes.


3️⃣Lean Expert – Design the System

A Lean Expert sees the organization as an interconnected system rather than isolated processes.

Minimum skills
• Lean deployment strategy
• Daily Management Systems
• Hoshin Kanri
• Leadership coaching
• Advanced problem solving
• Performance management and KPI design
• Organizational diagnosis
• Mentoring Lean Specialists

At this stage, technical expertise is expected, however influencing leaders becomes even more important.


4️⃣Lean Manager – Lead Through Lean

The Lean Manager is accountable for business performance, people development, and culture.

Minimum skills
• Strategic thinking
• Leadership and coaching
• Decision making
• Financial and business acumen
• Stakeholder management
• Talent development
• Conflict resolution
• Building a culture of continuous improvement

A Lean Manager isn’t measured by the number of Kaizen events delivered, but by the capability of the people they lead.


📈The Skill Evolution

The progression isn’t about learning more Lean tools.

It’s about expanding your capability:

Know the tools ⏩️ Teach the tools ⏩️ Design the system ⏩️ Develop people and deliver business results.

💥The higher you grow in Lean, the less your success depends on being the smartest problem solver in the room and the more it depends on enabling others to solve problems without you.

That’s when Lean stops being a methodology and becomes leadership.

Which of these four levels best describes where you are today? And what skill are you intentionally developing to reach the next level?

~Agnes

🌱🪴From Lean Practitioner to Lean Manager: It’s More Than a Job Title

I’ve noticed that organizations often use Lean titles replaceable:
Lean Practitioner
Lean Specialist
Lean Expert
Lean Manager
Yet these roles represent very different levels of responsibility, influence, and leadership.

A Lean career isn’t simply about learning more tools. It’s about expanding your impact from improving your own work to shaping an organization’s culture and business performance.

Here’s a practical way to distinguish these roles.

1️⃣Lean Practitioner – Applying Lean

Purpose: Improve your own work and contribute to continuous improvement.

Key responsibilities
• Apply Lean principles and standard work
• Identify waste and solve problems using PDCA or A3 thinking
• Participate in Kaizen activities
• Collect basic process data
• Sustain improvements and share ideas

Mandate
Improve the processes you own or work within while actively supporting your team’s improvement efforts.


2️⃣Lean Specialist – Facilitating Improvement

Purpose: Enable teams to improve.

Key responsibilities
• Lead Kaizen workshops
• Coach teams on Lean methods
• Train employees in Lean fundamentals
• Facilitate VSM and problem solving
• Develop visual management and monitor improvement metrics

Mandate
Lead improvement initiatives through facilitation, coaching, and influence rather than formal authority.


3️⃣Lean Expert – Driving Transformation

Purpose: Design Lean systems that support long-term business success.

Key responsibilities
• Develop Lean deployment strategies
• Coach leaders and managers
• Build Lean governance and operating systems
• Mentor Lean Specialists
• Align Lean initiatives with business strategy
• Remove systemic barriers to improvement

Mandate
Shape how Lean is implemented across functions and ensure improvements deliver sustainable business value.


4️⃣Lean Manager – Leading Through Lean

Purpose: Deliver business results by developing people and embedding Lean into daily leadership.

Key responsibilities
• Build high-performing teams
• Align improvement with strategic priorities
• Develop future Lean leaders
• Allocate resources effectively
• Create a culture of accountability, learning, and CI

Mandate
Lead people, make business decisions, and ensure Lean becomes the organization’s way of working, not just a collection of improvement projects.


⏩️The Progression

Lean Practitioner➡️ Specialist➡️ Expert➡️ Lean Manager

Apply➡️ Facilitate➡️ Transform➡️ Lead

The biggest shift is not technical expertise, it’s leadership.

* Practitioners improve their own work.
* Specialists improve processes with and through teams.
* Experts improve organizational systems.
* Managers improve business performance by developing people and creating the conditions for continuous improvement to thrive.

Lean is not a toolbox; it’s a leadership system. 

Organizations that clearly define these roles create stronger capabilities, clearer career paths, and more sustainable results.

⚠️“That’s how people from that country work.”
⚠️“It’s a cultural difference.”

🔻An excuse for weak communication.

🔻An excuse for not adapting.
🔻An excuse for accepting behavior that should simply be addressed.

Most companies don’t have a communication problem.

They have a missing function.

Everyone is doing exactly what they were hired to do.

And that’s where the problem begins.

Every department makes logical decisions from its own perspective. Individually, those decisions make sense. Collectively, they often create conflicting priorities, unnecessary complexity, expensive rework, delays, frustration, and stress.

Why?

Because very few organizations have an independent person or team responsible for looking at the business end-to-end.

Not another management layer.
Not another approval board.
Not another bureaucracy.

An experienced, independent function whose role is to connect the dots, challenge assumptions, identify cross-functional impacts, and ensure that important decisions have been considered from an end-to-end business perspective before they are implemented.

Not to make the decision.

But to ask the questions others often don’t.

1.Who else will this affect?
2.Have all impacted functions been involved?
3.Are we solving one problem while creating new ones somewhere else?
4.Is this decision truly aligned with the organization’s overall objectives?

These are simple questions.

The cost isn’t just financial.

🌱🪴🎯From Lean Practitioner to Lean Manager: What Skills Should Each Level Have?

In my previous article, I shared the different roles and responsibilities of a Lean Practitioner, Lean Specialist, Lean Expert, and Lean Manager.

A question followed naturally:
What are the minimum skills expected at each level?

While every organization has its own competency framework, I believe the progression should look something like this.

1️⃣Lean Practitioner – Learn and Apply

A Lean Practitioner doesn’t need to know every Lean tool. They need to understand why Lean exists and consistently apply its principles.

Minimum skills
• Understanding of Lean principles and the 8 wastes
• 5S, Visual Management and Standard Work
• Basic problem solving (PDCA, 5 Why)
• Ability to identify improvement opportunities
• Teamwork and willingness to learn
• Basic data collection and interpretation

At this level, curiosity and discipline are often more valuable than technical expertise.


2️⃣Lean Specialist – Coach and Facilitate

The Specialist’s role shifts from improving their own work to helping others improve.

Minimum skills
• Kaizen facilitation
• Value Stream Mapping
• Root Cause Analysis
• A3 thinking
• Training and coaching techniques
• Change management fundamentals
• Presentation and facilitation skills
• Basic project management

A great Specialist develops people, not just processes.


3️⃣Lean Expert – Design the System

A Lean Expert sees the organization as an interconnected system rather than isolated processes.

Minimum skills
• Lean deployment strategy
• Daily Management Systems
• Hoshin Kanri
• Leadership coaching
• Advanced problem solving
• Performance management and KPI design
• Organizational diagnosis
• Mentoring Lean Specialists

At this stage, technical expertise is expected, however influencing leaders becomes even more important.


4️⃣Lean Manager – Lead Through Lean

The Lean Manager is accountable for business performance, people development, and culture.

Minimum skills
• Strategic thinking
• Leadership and coaching
• Decision making
• Financial and business acumen
• Stakeholder management
• Talent development
• Conflict resolution
• Building a culture of continuous improvement

A Lean Manager isn’t measured by the number of Kaizen events delivered, but by the capability of the people they lead.


📈The Skill Evolution

The progression isn’t about learning more Lean tools.

It’s about expanding your capability:

Know the tools ⏩️ Teach the tools ⏩️ Design the system ⏩️ Develop people and deliver business results.

💥The higher you grow in Lean, the less your success depends on being the smartest problem solver in the room and the more it depends on enabling others to solve problems without you.

That’s when Lean stops being a methodology and becomes leadership.

Which of these four levels best describes where you are today? And what skill are you intentionally developing to reach the next level?

~Agnes

“𝘞𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯?”

It’s probably the question I’m asked most often.

Not:

“What is Lean?”

But:

“Which Lean tools should we implement first?”

My answer usually surprises people.

None.

At least not yet.

Because Lean is not a toolbox.

It’s a way of thinking.

Too many organizations start with 5S, Value Stream Mapping, Kanban, A3s, Kaizen boards, or visual management… hoping the tools will magically transform the business.

Months later they conclude:
“Lean doesn’t work here.”

The reality?

The tools weren’t the problem.

The mindset was.

Lean starts by understanding three simple questions:

✔️ What problem are we trying to solve?
✔️ What creates value for our customer?
✔️ What prevents us from delivering that value consistently?

Only then should we think about tools.

So where would I start?

Not with a tool.

I’d start by going to the place where the work happens.

Observe.
Listen.
Ask questions.

Talk to the people doing the work every day.

They usually know where the waste is.

If I had to choose only a few tools to begin with, they would be:

1. Gemba Walks
Go and see.
Don’t manage from PowerPoint.

2. Process Mapping
Understand the current reality before designing the future.

3. 5 Whys
Don’t fix symptoms.
Find the root cause.

4. Visual Management
Make problems visible instead of hiding them.

5. PDCA
Improve through small experiments, not big assumptions.

Notice something?

None of these tools are complicated.

Because Lean has never been about complexity.

It’s about developing a culture where people solve problems every day.

The biggest mistake isn’t choosing the wrong Lean tool.

It’s believing the tool will create the culture.

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘰𝘭𝘴 𝘴𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘺 𝘴𝘶𝘱𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵 𝘪𝘵.

So next time someone asks,

“Which Lean tool should we start with?”

Maybe the better question is:
“𝘈𝘳𝘦 𝘸𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘸𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬?”

I’d love to hear your experience.

If you were starting a Lean transformation tomorrow, what would be the very first thing you’d do?

~Agnes

🆘🛑We Measure Quality… But Are We Measuring the Right Thing?

Many people know me as a Lean enthusiast. And yes, I am passionate about Lean.

However Lean is much more than flow, waste, and efficiency. One of its strongest foundations is quality.

I’ve spent as many years working with quality as I have with Lean, and one thing has always surprised me.

Every organization measures quality in some way:
* Defects
* Errors
* Rework
* Customer complaints
* Scrap
* Cost of poor quality

We create dashboards, KPIs, Pareto charts, and monthly reports.

But 𝘐 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘴𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳, 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘳, 𝘦𝘯𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘳, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘲𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘧𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭:

𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘰𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘮𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘴?

𝘕𝘰𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘵𝘢𝘭 𝘯𝘶𝘮𝘣𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘧 𝘥𝘦𝘧𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘴.
𝘕𝘰𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘵 𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦.
𝘉𝘶𝘵 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘺’𝘴 𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘶𝘦𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢𝘭𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘺 𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘦.

Because that’s where the real story begins.

A defect that happens once might be an accident.
A defect that happens twice is a warning.
A defect that keeps returning is no longer a quality issue, it is a failure to learn.

If the same complaint appears every month, the problem isn’t the operator.
It isn’t the customer.
It isn’t bad luck.

The problem is that the organization solved the symptom instead of eliminating the root cause.

Reducing defects is good.

Preventing the same defect from ever happening again is what world-class organizations do.

So here’s my challenge to my network:

Do you measure repeat mistakes, repeat rework, and repeat complaints?
Because if you don’t know how many of your quality problems are recurring…

How can you honestly say your organization is improving?

⭐️1️⃣0️⃣ Qualities That Define an Exceptional Lean Manager!

Lean is often misunderstood as a collection of tools to reduce waste or improve efficiency. In reality, Lean is a way of thinking. The best Lean managers don’t simply implement processes they build cultures where people continuously solve problems, improve performance, and create value for customers.

🎯🌱Here are the 10 qualities that separate great Lean managers from the rest.

 1️⃣ They Lead by Example

A Lean manager never asks others to do what they wouldn’t do themselves. They demonstrate discipline, respect, accountability, and a commitment to continuous improvement through their own actions every day.

2️⃣ They Focus on Customer Value

Every decision starts with one question: Does this create value for the customer? Lean managers eliminate activities that don’t add value and ensure teams stay focused on what truly matters.

3️⃣ They Respect People

Lean is built on respect. Successful Lean leaders listen actively, empower employees, encourage ideas, and create an environment where everyone feels responsible for improvement.

4️⃣ They Embrace CI

The journey is never finished. Lean managers understand that every process can be improved, regardless of how well it performs today. Small, consistent improvements often lead to extraordinary results over time.

5️⃣ They Solve Problems at the Root Cause

Instead of treating symptoms, Lean managers investigate the real causes behind issues. They use structured problem-solving methods to prevent problems from recurring rather than repeatedly fixing the same mistakes.

6️⃣ They Make Decisions Based on Facts

Data guides decisions not assumptions. Effective Lean managers spend time observing processes, gathering evidence, and understanding reality before implementing solutions.

7️⃣ They Develop People

One of the greatest responsibilities of a Lean manager is coaching others. They invest in developing skills, encouraging learning, and helping employees become confident problem solvers.

8️⃣ They Communicate Clearly

Transparency builds trust. Lean managers share goals, expectations, performance metrics, and challenges openly, ensuring everyone understands priorities and how their work contributes to success.

9️⃣ They Think Systemically

Lean managers recognize that optimizing one department while hurting another is not improvement. They understand how processes connect across the entire value stream and focus on improving the whole system.

🔟 They Stay Humble and Curious

The best Lean leaders know they don’t have all the answers. They ask questions, seek feedback, learn from failures, and remain open to new ideas. Their curiosity drives innovation and continuous learning.

🔔 Lesson learned 

Lean management is not about achieving perfection, it’s about pursuing it every single day. The most effective Lean managers combine technical knowledge with strong leadership, empathy, and a genuine passion for developing people.

🔔The Biggest Mistake Many Organizations Keep Making

I’ve seen it too many times, and it still surprises me.

A company is struggling with poor quality, customer complaints, and rising operational costs. The cost of poor quality reaches millions every year.

So what does management do?

They decide to reduce costs by letting go of their most experienced experts the very people who understand the processes, know the customers, and have spent years solving complex problems.

Why?

Because they are “too expensive.”
Instead, they hire less experienced people simply because they cost less.
On paper, it looks like a smart financial decision.

💥In reality, it’s often one of the most expensive decisions an organization can make.

𝘌𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘢 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵.
𝘐𝘵 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵.

𝘞𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘭𝘬𝘴 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘰𝘳, 𝘴𝘰 𝘥𝘰 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘭𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘥, 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮-𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘴, 𝘤𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘳 𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺. 𝘛𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨𝘴 𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘣𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵.

Unfortunately, I see the same pattern with Lean.

Leadership announces a Lean transformation because they want better performance and lower costs.

But instead of investing in experienced Lean professionals who can build a sustainable culture, they hire the cheapest option just to show that “something is happening.”

Lean is not about ticking a box.
Lean is not about hiring the lowest bidder.

𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬𝘴, 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘰𝘶𝘴𝘭𝘺 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘴. 𝘛𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘲𝘶𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘴 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦, 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦, 𝘤𝘰𝘢𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺.

Choosing someone simply because they are cheaper may save money today but it often creates much bigger costs tomorrow:
♨️More quality issues.
♨️More customer complaints.
♨️More rework.
♨️More firefighting.
♨️Lower employee engagement.
♨️Lost customer trust.

The irony?

𝘖𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘧𝘪𝘹𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘺 𝘬𝘦𝘦𝘱𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘰𝘳 𝘩𝘪𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘦.


𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘲𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴, 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘴𝘦 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯.

𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘧𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨.

And eventually, the bill always arrives.

The question is:
When will organizations stop treating experience as an expense instead of one of their greatest competitive advantages?

I’d love to hear your thoughts. Have you seen this happen in your organization?

⛑️🧰Have you ever noticed something interesting?

We spend a lot of time talking about how to onboard new employees. We create welcome packages, training plans, buddy systems, and first-90-day roadmaps. But we rarely ask an equally important question:

How do you onboard a Lean Specialist?

The answer isn’t as obvious as it seems.

A Lean expert can become one of the biggest drivers of improvement or one of the fastest ways to create resistance. The difference often has little to do with technical knowledge and everything to do with how the organization introduces the role.

📍Scenario 1: Lean doesn’t exist yet

This is both the easiest and the hardest situation.

There are no previous failures to overcome, but there are also no success stories. Expectations can quickly become unrealistic. Many leaders expect the new Lean Specialist to “fix the company” within a few months.

The reality is different.

The first responsibility is not to launch dozens of improvement projects. It is to understand the business.

A Lean Specialist should spend time on the shop floor, talk with operators, engineers, supervisors, maintenance teams, logistics, and office functions. Observe before proposing. Learn before teaching.

Only after understanding the culture, challenges, and daily work should the first improvement initiatives begin.

The first wins should be small, visible, and solve real problems for employees not just improve KPIs on a dashboard.

📍Scenario 2: Lean already exists

This is often more challenging.

The new Lean Specialist doesn’t start with a blank page. They inherit existing standards, projects, successes, failures, and, most importantly, opinions.

Before changing anything, it’s worth asking:

* Why do we work this way?
* What has already been tried?
* What worked?
* What failed?
* What frustrates people about Lean today?

Many organizations make the mistake of expecting every new Lean expert to introduce their own tools immediately.

But Lean is not about leaving your personal signature everywhere.

Sometimes the biggest improvement is continuing what already works while helping people improve it further.

Respect for people also means respecting the organization’s history.

The first 90 days matter

Whether Lean is new or already established, I believe the first months should focus on:

✅ Building relationships before driving change.
✅ Listening more than presenting.
✅ Understanding the business before selecting tools.
✅ Finding quick wins that matter to employees.
✅ Creating trust instead of pushing methodologies.

Lean tools are relatively easy to learn.

Building credibility takes much longer.

The biggest misconception

Companies often hire a Lean Specialist expecting immediate transformation.

But Lean transformation is never the responsibility of one person.

The Lean Specialist facilitates, coaches, and develops problem-solving capabilities.

Real improvement happens only when leaders and employees own the change together.

‼️I Won’t Fix a Broken System

𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘢 𝘱𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘵 𝘪𝘯 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶’𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘰 𝘭𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘦𝘳 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴, 𝘺𝘰𝘶’𝘷𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘢𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘬𝘦𝘦𝘱𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘷𝘦.

I’ve seen organizations where talented people work harder every quarter, attend more meetings, produce more reports, and implement more processes. Yet somehow, nothing really improves.

The system isn’t underperforming because people aren’t trying hard enough.

♨️The system is broken.

Too often, leadership responds by asking individuals to compensate:
* Work longer.
* Be more resilient.
* Communicate better.
* Take more ownership.

But 𝘢𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘹𝘤𝘦𝘱𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘺 𝘥𝘺𝘴𝘧𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘴𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘪𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘱. 𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘴𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵.

High performers eventually burn out.
Average performers adapt.
Innovation disappears.

The uncomfortable truth is this:

𝘈 𝘣𝘳𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯 𝘴𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘮 𝘳𝘦𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘴 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯, 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘪𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘰𝘴𝘪𝘵𝘺.

You cannot coach your way out of bad incentives.
You cannot motivate people past conflicting priorities.
And you certainly cannot automate broken thinking.

Technology—including AI—doesn’t solve dysfunctional organizations.

It scales them.

If your processes are inefficient, AI makes inefficient processes faster.
If your decisions are biased, AI amplifies those biases.
If your culture discourages questioning, technology simply accelerates silence.

Real transformation begins somewhere far less exciting than a new tool or a new strategy.

It begins with asking difficult questions:
* Why do we do this?
* Who actually benefits?
* What would we design if we started today?
* Which rules are protecting value and which are protecting comfort?

Sometimes the bravest thing a leader can say isn’t “Let’s optimize this.”

🚨It’s:
“Let’s stop doing it.”

The future doesn’t belong to organizations that work the hardest.

It belongs to those willing to redesign the system instead of asking people to survive it.

I no longer aspire to fix broken systems.
I aspire to build better ones.

Because people deserve systems that help them succeed, not systems that require them to sacrifice themselves just to keep them running.


Question to my Network:
⁉️What’s one process in your organization that everyone accepts as “normal,” even though deep down everyone knows it’s broken?

🎭 Lean Theatre vs. Real Lean — Part 2
Last week I wrote about Lean Theatre.

𝘔𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘴𝘢𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨:

“𝘐 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘸𝘦’𝘳𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘳𝘦… 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘥𝘰 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘱?”

The answer isn’t another tool.

It’s changing the questions leaders ask.

Most organizations are full of leaders who ask:
❌ Is the KPI green?
❌ Did everyone attend the meeting?
❌ Was the audit completed?
❌ Is the action plan finished?

Those questions create compliance.
Lean leaders ask different questions.

Instead of asking:
“Who made the mistake?”

they ask:
“What in the process allowed this to happen?”

Instead of:
“Did we complete the improvement project?”

they ask:
“What capability did we build?”

Instead of:
“Who owns this problem?”

they ask:
“Who learned to solve it?”

Because Lean isn’t about fixing today’s issue.
It’s about making tomorrow’s problem easier to solve.

𝘛𝘩𝘢𝘵’𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘺 𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘭𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘨𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘴…
…𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴.

Not because they don’t know the answer.
Because every answer they give creates dependency.

Every good question builds capability.
The real measure of leadership isn’t:

“How many problems did I solve today?”

It’s:
“How many problems can my team solve tomorrow without me?”

That shift changes everything.
Meetings become coaching sessions.
KPIs become learning tools.
Gemba becomes a classroom.
Managers become teachers.

And improvement stops being an event…
…and becomes the way people think.

Lean has never been about creating experts.
It’s about creating thousands of expert problem solvers.

That’s how organizations become resilient.

Not because leaders are always present.

But because capability is.

Question for leaders:
Think about the last problem your team brought to you.

Did you give them the answer…
…or did you help them discover it?

The difference is where Lean begins.

Most leaders don’t become “part of the solution” overnight. They become it by recognizing they are still somewhere on the left side, and deciding to move.

Every leader agrees with the right side.

The real question is: Where are you today?

When I shared previous article and visual, I realized something.

Almost every leader who sees it will immediately look to the green side.

“Yes, that’s leadership.”
“Absolutely.”
“100% agree.”
And this were feedback.

Very few will willingly point to the red side and say:

“That’s me.”

And that’s completely human.

None of us wake up intending to blame people instead of solving problems.
None of us schedule meetings hoping to avoid reality.
None of us choose assumptions over facts.

Yet many organizations slowly drift there.

Not because leaders are bad.
Because leadership is difficult.


The interesting part isn’t choosing between the left and the right.

It’s understanding that the right side isn’t a destination.
It’s a direction.

Every great leader started somewhere left of it.
The difference is that they were willing to admit it.

Because improvement always begins with one uncomfortable sentence:

“Maybe I am part of this problem.”

That isn’t weakness.
That’s leadership.


The biggest obstacle to becoming better isn’t capability.

It’s believing you’re already there.
If you think you’re already the leader on the green side…

Why would you change?
Why would you ask for feedback?
Why would you go to the Gemba?
Why would you challenge your own decisions?


Toyota never expected perfect leaders.

It expected leaders who learned.
Who observed before judging.
Who listened before deciding.
Who coached instead of controlled.
Who solved problems instead of assigning blame.

Leadership isn’t about never standing on the left.
It’s about spending less and less time there.



So perhaps the real daily leadership question isn’t:

“Am I part of the solution?”

It’s:

“What is one thing I can do today that moves me one step to the right?”

Because better is always an option.
But improvement never starts with agreement.

It starts with honesty.



What was the moment in your leadership journey when you realized you needed to move a little further to the right?

I’d love to hear your experience.

⚠️ 🔔𝘙𝘦𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘗𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘈𝘭𝘴𝘰 𝘔𝘦𝘢𝘯𝘴 𝘙𝘦𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘓𝘪𝘮𝘪𝘵𝘴 

We talk a lot about resilience.

“Never give up.”
“Keep pushing.”
“Try harder.”
“Find a way.”

It sounds inspiring.

Until it isn’t.

⁉️What we rarely talk about is where the boundary is.

At what point does perseverance stop being a strength and become waste?
How long should someone keep giving 110% when the system keeps taking 120%?

In Lean, we are taught to eliminate waste.

Yet 𝘸𝘦 𝘰𝘧𝘵𝘦𝘯 𝘤𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘣𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘣𝘪𝘨𝘨𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘸𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘢𝘭𝘭:

𝘞𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘩𝘶𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘱𝘰𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘭.

Not because people don’t try.
Because they keep trying in systems that refuse to change.

There is a difference between persistence and stubbornness.
Between commitment and self-sacrifice.
Between solving problems and repeatedly absorbing them.

A great leader doesn’t ask people to keep compensating for broken systems.
A great leader fixes the system.

Sometimes the bravest decision isn’t to push harder.

It’s to stop.

To say:
“This process is broken.”
“This expectation is unrealistic.”
“This is no longer creating value.”

Respect for People isn’t asking someone to give more.
It’s knowing when they have already given enough.

⁉️So here’s my question to leaders:

𝘏𝘰𝘸 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘰𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦… 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘣𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘵𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺’𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘷𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨?

Because burnout is not commitment.

Constant firefighting is not Operational Excellence.

And endless effort is not a strategy.

𝘚𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘥𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘦…
𝘪𝘴 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘱 𝘱𝘶𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘪𝘨𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨.

⚔️ 𝘊𝘩𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘯𝘨𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘚𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘶𝘴 𝘘𝘶𝘰

Every organization has one invisible rule.

“We’ve always done it this way.”

It rarely appears in a procedure.
You’ll never find it in an SOP.
It’s not part of the strategy.

Yet it silently influences thousands of decisions every day.

It stops people from asking why.
It discourages experimentation.
It rewards compliance over curiosity.

And slowly, improvement becomes maintenance.

The status quo isn’t dangerous because it’s wrong.

It’s dangerous because it feels comfortable.

History has never been changed by people protecting what already exists.

Every breakthrough…
Every innovation…
Every improvement…
Started with someone willing to challenge what everyone else accepted as normal.

As leaders, our responsibility isn’t to preserve today’s way of working.

It’s to create tomorrow’s.

That doesn’t mean changing everything.

It means having the courage to ask questions such as:

𝘞𝘩𝘺 𝘥𝘰 𝘸𝘦 𝘥𝘰 𝘪𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘢𝘺?
𝘐𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘷𝘢𝘭𝘶𝘦?
𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘸𝘦 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘵𝘳𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘷𝘦?
𝘐𝘧 𝘸𝘦 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘪𝘨𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘺, 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘸𝘦 𝘣𝘶𝘪𝘭𝘥 𝘪𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘺?

In Lean. We often talk about eliminating waste.

But 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘸𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘤𝘤𝘦𝘱𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘥𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘺 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘪𝘵 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘦𝘹𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘴.

🚨A standard should be the best known way today, not a permanent monument to yesterday.

So don’t be afraid to challenge the status quo.

Pick up the sword of curiosity.
Cut through assumptions.
Question habits.
Remove unnecessary complexity.

Because continuous improvement begins the moment someone is brave enough to say:

“𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘩𝘢𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘢 𝘣𝘦𝘵𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘢𝘺.”

⚔️ Challenge the status quo. Respect people. Improve the system.

What is one “we’ve always done it this way” practice in your organization that deserves to be challenged?

💎📍🕸️The Most Important Team Almost Every Organization Is Missing

After more than 20 years of working across different organizations, I’ve come to a conclusion that may sound controversial:

Most companies don’t have a communication problem.
They don’t even have a silo problem.

They have a missing function.

Every organization has talented specialists. Finance optimizes financial. Operations improve efficiency. IT delivers technology. Sales drive growth. HR focuses on people.

Everyone is doing exactly what they were hired to do.

And that’s where the problem begins.

Every department makes logical decisions from its own perspective. Individually, those decisions make sense. Collectively, they often create conflicting priorities, unnecessary complexity, expensive rework, delays, frustration, and stress.

Why?

Because very few organizations have an independent person or team responsible for looking at the business end-to-end.

Not another management layer.
Not another approval board.
Not another bureaucracy.

An experienced, independent function whose role is to connect the dots, challenge assumptions, identify cross-functional impacts, and ensure that important decisions have been considered from an end-to-end business perspective before they are implemented.

Not to make the decision.

But to ask the questions others often don’t.

* Who else will this affect?
* Have all impacted functions been involved?
* Are we solving one problem while creating new ones somewhere else?
* Is this decision truly aligned with the organization’s overall objectives?

These are simple questions.

Yet they are often asked only after the damage is done.

The consequences are familiar to all of us: projects redesigned months later, disconnected processes, departments blaming each other, wasted budgets, unnecessary stress.

The cost isn’t just financial.

It weakens trust, slows execution, and makes collaboration harder with every avoidable mistake.

I’m not suggesting someone should know every detail of every process. That’s impossible.

But it is absolutely possible to build an independent capability with broad business knowledge, strong end-to-end understanding, and enough experience to see risks, dependencies, and unintended consequences before they become expensive.

Organizations invest millions in AI, digital transformation, new systems, and consultants.

Yet many still overlook the capability that could significantly increase the success of every one of those investments: independent end-to-end alignment.

After 20 years, I no longer believe organizations fail because they lack smart people.

They fail because smart people make isolated decisions while no one is truly responsible for protecting the whole.

The organizations that will outperform tomorrow won’t just have the best specialists.

They’ll have the people who connect everything together.

End-to-end thinking isn’t a luxury. It’s one of the greatest competitive advantages an organization can build.

🚨🧨𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘐 𝘓𝘰𝘷𝘦 𝘓𝘶𝘤𝘺 𝘊𝘢𝘯 𝘛𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘩 𝘜𝘴 𝘈𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘋𝘢𝘴𝘩𝘣𝘰𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘴, 𝘈𝘯𝘢𝘭𝘺𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘖𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴

 I had several times meetings that many operational leaders know all too well.

A dashboard was presented as “working perfectly.”

The numbers looked clean.
The charts looked impressive.
The message to leadership was simple:

“Everything works properly.”

Except…

Operations lives in reality, not in PowerPoint.

It reminded me of I Love Lucy.

Whether Lucy was trying to keep up with an impossible production line or learning the hard way in Italy that reality doesn’t always match expectations, the lesson was always the same:

Looking busy is not the same as understanding the work.

The same happens with many operational dashboards.

Someone who has never managed or even never step in to shopfloor…
Never worked a shift…
Never chased an OTD target…
Never dealt with inventory discrepancies…
Never experienced the consequences of a delayed truck…

…designs a dashboard and decides what Operations should measure.🔮⁉️

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘮𝘶𝘭𝘢𝘴 𝘮𝘢𝘺 𝘣𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘵.

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘷𝘪𝘴𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘮𝘢𝘺 𝘣𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘢𝘶𝘵𝘪𝘧𝘶𝘭.

…𝘉𝘶𝘵 𝘪𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘭𝘰𝘨𝘪𝘤 𝘣𝘦𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘢𝘵𝘢 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴𝘯’𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘵 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘴, 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘢𝘴𝘩𝘣𝘰𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘥𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘦𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘴:

𝘈 𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘳.🧨

This is why Operation has always started at the Gemba.

Not because operators know Excel better.
Not because analysts are less intelligent.

But because reality lives where the work happens.

Analytics should never replace operational knowledge.

They should amplify it.

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘥𝘢𝘴𝘩𝘣𝘰𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘴 𝘐’𝘷𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘣𝘶𝘪𝘭𝘵 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘖𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴.

𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘣𝘶𝘪𝘭𝘵 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘖𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴.

𝘈𝘯𝘢𝘭𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘴 𝘣𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘥𝘢𝘵𝘢 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘴𝘦.

𝘖𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘣𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘴𝘦.

𝘛𝘰𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘣𝘶𝘪𝘭𝘵 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘴𝘵.

Because the purpose of a dashboard isn’t to make leadership feel comfortable.

Its purpose is to expose reality even when reality is uncomfortable.

⁉️So before telling your BOSS that everything works perfectly, ask one simple question:

“𝘏𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘳𝘶𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘥𝘢𝘺 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘮𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘥𝘢𝘴𝘩𝘣𝘰𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘴 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺?”

Because if the answer is no…

You may not have a dashboard.

🚨You may simply have a very expensive illusion.

Data without operational understanding creates beautiful reports.

Operational understanding combined with good analytics creates better decisions.

There is a world of difference.

🌱💎 𝘚𝘵𝘰𝘱 𝘚𝘱𝘦𝘯𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘔𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘠𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘛𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘰𝘯 𝘠𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘉𝘪𝘨𝘨𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘗𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴.

𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐛𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐩𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥.

I recently watched a podcast that shared an interesting way of looking at organizational performance.

Imagine your company has 200 employees.

The square root of 200 is roughly 14–15 people (often rounded in examples to around 16).

The idea is that this surprisingly small group generates a disproportionately large share of the company’s value. Whether or not the exact numbers hold for every organization, the underlying leadership lesson is powerful.

Then think about the Pareto Principle.

Roughly 20% of your people often contribute to a large share of the results.

These are not just your top performers.

They are the people who:
✔️solve problems before they become crises,
✔️influence others without asking for authority,
✔️improve standards instead of working around them,
✔️carry the culture when no one is watching,
✔️make everyone around them better.

Yet where do many organizations spend most of their leadership time?

🔻On poor performers.
🔻On constant firefighting.
🔻On fixing the same problems.
🔻On endless performance conversations with people who have already decided not to improve.

⚠️ Meanwhile, the people carrying the business quietly continue doing exactly that… carrying the business.

Without recognition.
Without mentoring.
Without investment.
Without a clear development path.

Eventually someone else notices them.

And they leave.

As a Lean leader, I believe this is one of the biggest strategic mistakes organizations make.

„𝘠𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘩𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘢𝘵𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘣𝘪𝘨𝘨𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴.”

That doesn’t mean ignoring underperformance.

It means understanding where your greatest return on leadership investment truly is.

Find your emerging leaders.

Coach them.

Challenge them.

Give them difficult projects.

Invest in their development.

Teach them how to lead others.

Protect them from burnout.

Because the future performance of your organization will not be determined by how much time you spend managing your weakest employees.

It will be determined by how well you develop the people capable of building the next generation of leaders.

Don’t only ask:
“Who needs fixing?”

Start asking:
“Who deserves more investment?”

That question may change the future of your company.


⁉️Leadership Challenge

If tomorrow your five strongest people accepted offers somewhere else…

Would your organization continue improving?

Or would it simply continue holding more meetings?

I recently watched an old interview with Taiichi Ohno.

No PowerPoint.
No AI.
No digital dashboards.
No fancy Lean vocabulary.

Just clear thinking.

And while watching it, I kept asking myself one question:

𝘐𝘧 𝘛𝘢𝘪𝘪𝘤𝘩𝘪 𝘖𝘩𝘯𝘰 𝘸𝘢𝘭𝘬𝘦𝘥 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘰 𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘺… 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘩 𝘶𝘴?

Probably not another Lean tool.
Probably not another certification.
Probably not another workshop.

He would ask uncomfortable questions.

⁉️Why are managers discussing problems in meeting rooms instead of at the Gemba?
⁉️Why do we measure activity instead of customer value?
⁉️Why do we celebrate busy people instead of improving processes?
⁉️Why do we build reports instead of solving problems?
⁉️Why do we automate waste before eliminating it?

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘐 𝘭𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘥, 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘐 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘦𝘥 𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘵.
𝘔𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘰𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦𝘯’𝘵 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘯.
𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘺’𝘷𝘦 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺’𝘷𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨.

Today we have AI.
Real-time dashboards.
Predictive analytics.
Digital twins.
Automated workflows.

Yet many organizations still struggle with the same problems Toyota was solving more than 50 years ago.

Why?

Because technology never fixes poor thinking.

Taiichi Ohno never started with software.

He started with observation.

He didn’t ask,
“What system should we buy?”

He asked,
“Why does this waste exist?”

He didn’t build Lean around tools.
He built it around curiosity.
He didn’t ask people to work faster.
He designed systems where working smarter became natural.

⚠️Perhaps the biggest lesson from the video is this:
Lean was never about manufacturing.
It was about leadership.

🎯Leaders who go and see.
🎯Leaders who challenge assumptions.
🎯Leaders who develop people instead of creating dependence.
🎯Leaders who understand that every inventory pile, every delay, every workaround and every defect is simply a symptom of a deeper problem waiting to be understood.

Today many companies invest millions in digital transformation.

But imagine if they invested the same energy in teaching leaders how to observe.

How to ask better questions.
How to think scientifically.
How to solve problems at the root.

That would be a transformation no software could replace.

If Taiichi Ohno walked into your organization today…

I don’t think he would ask to see your dashboards.

I think he would ask one simple question:
“Show me where the work happens.”

Because that’s where improvement has always started.

Not in the boardroom.
Not in PowerPoint.
Not in AI.

At the Gemba.
And perhaps that lesson is more relevant today than ever.

Leaders, answer one question honestly.

𝘈𝘳𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘶𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯… 𝘰𝘳 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮?

𝘕𝘰𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘮.

𝘕𝘰𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘮𝘢𝘯𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘳𝘴.

𝘕𝘰𝘵 𝘏𝘙.

𝘕𝘰𝘵 𝘖𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴.

𝘠𝘰𝘶.

Every organization has problems.

Poor quality.
Missed deliveries.
High turnover.
Firefighting.
Low engagement.
Slow decisions.

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭 𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴:
𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘥𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘬𝘦𝘦𝘱𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘷𝘦?

As leaders, we love asking:
* Why aren’t people following the standard?
* Why don’t they take ownership?
* Why isn’t Lean working?
* Why is nobody speaking up?

But how often do we ask ourselves:
* Do I create psychological safety?
* Do I spend time at the Gemba?
* Do I remove obstacles or create them?
* Do I make decisions based on facts or assumptions?
* Do I reward learning or only results?
* Do I solve root causes or just demand faster fixes?

The culture of an organization rarely grows beyond the behavior of its leaders.

If leaders ignore standards, people will too.
If leaders avoid difficult conversations, everyone else will.
If leaders chase blame instead of understanding, problems simply become better hidden.

Leadership is not measured by the number of meetings you attend or presentations you give.

It is measured by the problems you help people solve.

So before asking your team to improve…

𝘚𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘯 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘪𝘳𝘳𝘰𝘳 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘴𝘬 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘴𝘦𝘭𝘧:
𝘈𝘮 𝘐 𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘶𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘺’𝘴 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘴… 𝘰𝘳 𝘢𝘤𝘤𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘳𝘰𝘸’𝘴? 

Because every leader is part of the system.

And every day, they choose whether to become part of the solution, or part of the problem.

The hardest Gemba walk is sometimes the one into your own leadership.

🎭🎪Lean Theatre vs. Real Lean

Walk into almost any company today and you’ll find Lean.

There are boards.
There are KPIs.
There are daily meetings.
There are audits.
There are improvement projects.

On paper, everything looks impressive.

Yet somehow…

The same problems return every week.
The same leaders make the same decisions.
The same firefighting continues.
The same people become the heroes who keep saving broken systems.

That’s not Lean.

That’s Lean theatre.

Real Lean isn’t measured by how many tools you implement.

It’s measured by how few problems depend on one person.

A real Lean organization looks different:

✅ Leaders start their day at the Gemba, not in PowerPoint.
✅ Problems become visible immediately instead of being hidden.
✅ Standards help people succeed instead of collecting dust in folders.
✅ KPIs trigger action, not discussions.
✅ Managers develop people instead of becoming the solution to every problem.
✅ Decisions are based on facts from the Gemba, not opinions from meeting rooms.

And there is one simple test that reveals everything.

Go on holiday.

If your phone never stops ringing…
If every decision waits for your approval…
If improvement stops until you return…

You haven’t built a Lean system.

You’ve built dependency.

The purpose of Lean has never been to make one person indispensable.

Its purpose is exactly the opposite.

To build people.
To build capability.
To build systems that continue improving even when the leader isn’t there.

Because the greatest Lean achievement isn’t becoming the hero.

It’s creating an organization that no longer needs one.


Question for leaders:

If you disappeared for two weeks tomorrow…

Would your operation survive… or continue to improve?

💜🎯🌱The Best Leadership Lesson I’ve Seen in a Long Time

I watched a short video today.

Less than a minute.

Yet it contained more leadership wisdom than many full-day conferences.

It reminded me of something we’ve forgotten in many organizations:

Leadership isn’t about explaining why something can’t be done. It’s about taking responsibility for making it happen.

Too often I see leaders who:

* own meetings instead of problems,
* own presentations instead of results,
* own opinions instead of decisions.

Real leaders do something different.

They don’t ask:
“Whose fault is this?”

They ask:
“What do we do next?”

They don’t wait for another report.
They go to the Gemba.

They don’t blame the system.
They improve it.

They don’t ask employees to be accountable for things they themselves avoid.
That’s why people follow leaders not because of their title, but because of their behavior.

Every employee watches what a leader tolerates.
Every employee notices which standards are ignored.
Every employee learns what is truly important not from PowerPoint slides, but from daily actions.

The strongest leadership message is never spoken.

It is demonstrated.

Sometimes, one minute of truth is worth more than one hundred hours of corporate training.

Question for leaders:

If your team copied everything you did this week, would your organization become better… or just busier?

Lean starts with leaders who lead by example not by exception.

— Agnes

🚨💥Helping or Hiding the Problem?

I recently listened to an interesting podcast by Cole DaSilva, and one sentence stayed with me:

“𝘠𝘰𝘶’𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘰𝘸𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘱𝘪𝘤𝘬 𝘶𝘱 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘬 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘤𝘰-𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘦𝘳𝘴. 𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘬𝘦𝘦𝘱 𝘥𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘦𝘭𝘴𝘦’𝘴 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬, 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘸𝘦 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘺 𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦?”

At first, it sounds harsh.

However the more I thought about it…

The more I realized how often this happens in organizations.
There is almost always that one employee.
The one everyone depends on.
The one who stays late.
The one who fixes mistakes.
The one who quietly finishes work that someone else left behind.

⚡️Leadership calls them a high performer.
⚡️Their colleagues call them helpful.

But here’s the uncomfortable question:
Are they helping… or are they hiding the problem?

Every time a strong employee compensates for poor performance, the organization loses visibility.

The KPIs look acceptable.
Customers receive their orders.
The shift finishes on time.
Managers think everything is under control.

But it isn’t.

The system isn’t working.

One person is simply carrying the weight of everyone else.

Lean teaches us to make problems visible.

Yet many organizations unknowingly reward the people who make problems invisible.

Helping each other is essential.

That is teamwork.

But there is a difference between supporting your team and permanently covering for a broken system or repeated poor performance.

If someone occasionally needs help, great teams step in.
If someone constantly needs saving, leaders need to ask why.

Is it training?
Is it unclear expectations?
Is it poor leadership?
Or is it simply the wrong fit for the role?

Respect for People doesn’t mean lowering standards.

It means giving everyone the opportunity to succeed, and having the courage to address performance when they don’t.

Because the strongest team isn’t built around one hero.
It’s built around people who can all be trusted to do their part.
A great organization doesn’t need one person carrying ten others.

It builds ten people who are capable of carrying themselves and helping each other when it truly matters.

Helping should strengthen the team.

Not hide the problems leadership needs to solve.

Cole DaSilva 💜🌱🙏🏻

“Never become the Godfather of your organization.”

Many leaders unknowingly become exactly that.

Everyone comes to them for:
* Every decision.
* Every approval.
* Every problem.
* Every conflict.

At first, it feels like leadership.

In reality, it’s a bottleneck.

If every road leads to one office, you don’t have a management system you have dependency.

Lean asks leaders to build systems that solve problems without needing “the Godfather.”



Other powerful metaphors include:

🤝 Loyalty vs. Capability

The Godfather values loyalty above almost everything.

Lean values capability first.

Loyal people who cannot solve problems will never build a great organization.

Develop people so they can think, not just obey.



🤫 Information is Power

In The Godfather, information is closely guarded.

In Lean, information is visual, transparent, and shared.

Visual Management exists so everyone can see reality not just senior leaders.



👀 Respect Over Fear

Many obey the Godfather because they fear him.

Lean organizations improve because people feel safe enough to speak up.

Fear hides problems.

Respect reveals them.



🔥 Solving the Symptom

In the film, many conflicts are “solved” by removing people.

Lean removes the process that created the problem.

People are rarely the root cause.

Systems usually are.



👑 Succession

The Godfather worries constantly about who comes next.

Lean builds successors every day.

A great leader creates more leaders not more followers.



My private message:

If your organization cannot function without you, you’ve built dependence not leadership.

That’s one of the deepest Lean lessons.

The ultimate goal of Lean leadership isn’t to become indispensable.

It’s to build people and systems that no longer depend on you.

That is when you know you’ve truly succeeded.
